presentation.teaser: On foreign influence in education, Foushee opposed two bills that would cut off specified federal funding to schools or colleges over certain China-linked ties or Chinese-government-backed support. She also supported a proposed replacement version of H.R. 1048 that would require detailed foreign-gift and contract reporting, public disclosure, and penalties for some violations. She later opposed the broader final H.R. 1048 package, so that vote does not show which part of the final bill she rejected.

presentation.scope_boundary: This preview covers Valerie Foushee's reviewed 119th-Congress Education & Workforce record.

notable_choices.title: Supported a reporting-focused replacement, opposed the final H.R. 1048 package
limitations: The final H.R. 1048 vote applied to the whole package and does not show which provision Foushee opposed.
notable_choices.public_title: Supported a reporting-focused replacement, opposed the final H.R. 1048 package
notable_choices.primary_sentence: Foushee supported a proposed replacement version of H.R. 1048 that would set foreign-gift and contract reporting thresholds for colleges, make reports publicly searchable, allow some equivalent reporting and specified exclusions, and impose fines or compliance plans for some violations. She then opposed the broader final H.R. 1048 package, which also included contract restrictions and other reporting and enforcement provisions. The final vote does not identify which part she opposed.

repeated_patterns.title: Opposed two China-linked education funding restrictions
limitations: H.R. 881 concerned Department of Homeland Security funding for colleges, while H.R. 1069 concerned covered federal education funds for K–12 schools. Neither covered all federal funding.
The bills covered different China-linked relationships and used different waiver rules; H.R. 1069's funding restriction would begin one year after enactment.
repeated_patterns.public_title: Opposed two China-linked education funding restrictions
repeated_patterns.primary_sentence: Foushee opposed H.R. 881, which would generally make colleges with specified ties to named China-linked programs or entities ineligible for Department of Homeland Security funding, and H.R. 1069, which would generally withhold covered federal education funds from K–12 schools with specified Chinese-government-backed partnerships or resources. Both bills included waiver routes, but they covered different sectors, funding streams, and conditions.

repeated_patterns.title: Supported keeping collective bargaining in force
limitations: H.R. 2550 concerned federal and Foreign Service labor-management rules, while H.R. 5408 concerned private-sector collective bargaining under federal labor law.
Preserving existing federal union agreements is different from maintaining employment terms and a duty to bargain during first-contract negotiations.
H.R. 5408 also required mediation and binding arbitration; support for either whole bill does not show which individual provision drove Foushee's vote.
repeated_patterns.public_title: Supported keeping collective bargaining in force
repeated_patterns.primary_sentence: Foushee supported H.R. 2550, which would reverse a 2025 executive order that excluded specified federal agencies and units from federal or Foreign Service labor-management rules and preserve covered union agreements already in effect. She also supported H.R. 5408, which would require continued bargaining and unchanged employment terms while workers' representatives and employers negotiated a first contract, with mediation and binding arbitration if talks remained unresolved.

caveats: The parental-consent clause is limited to minors in elementary or middle grades and the listed school-form changes or sex-based accommodations. The separate use-of-funds prohibition applies to ESEA funds and is not confined by that clause's definition of a covered student.

EO14168 section 2 defines sex as an unchangeable male/female biological classification and defines gender identity separately; subsection (f) supplies the incorporated gender-ideology definition. That definition also describes requiring institutions to recognize identification as a different sex as establishing that sex. This explanation attributes those classifications to the legal text, without adopting the order's evaluative descriptions or treating its rhetoric as established fact.

The bill prohibits teaching or advancing concepts related to the incorporated definition. It does not enumerate particular lessons, books or classroom scenarios; the candidate does not invent such applications. Incorporating this definition does not import all other Executive Order directives, and this whole-package choice is not projected onto separate component votes.
exact_action_receipts.policy_question: Public schools receiving ESEA funds would need parental consent for specified school-form or bathroom/locker-room changes involving minors in elementary or middle grades. These are the Executive Order's incorporated categories, not Political Fingerprint's judgments about gender.

caveats: Title 5 exclusions cover State, Defense, Treasury except the Bureau of Engraving and Printing, Veterans Affairs, Justice, Energy except FERC, EPA, USAID, NRC, NSF, USITC, FCC, and GSA. They also cover listed HHS, DHS, Interior and Agriculture units, Commerce's International Trade Administration, and specified information-resource-management offices across executive departments, SSA and OPM. The exact subdivisions are retained in the structured source excerpts, not generalized to all employees of every listed department.

The order retains Chapter 71 coverage for immediate local employing offices of police officers, security guards and firefighters, except the Bureau of Prisons, and for specified Marshals Service subdivisions. Defense and VA secretaries could restore coverage to subdivisions through certified orders submitted for Federal Register publication within 15 days. Transportation received a separate, non-redelegable power to exclude subdivisions, including FAA, or suspend provisions for certain overseas activities after published determinations; the order does not itself exclude every Transportation employee.

Foreign Service exclusions cover State subdivisions under the named senior offices plus embassies, consulates, diplomatic missions and consular offices, and USAID overseas missions/field offices and specified administrator/deputy-administrator subdivisions. The complete lists are in EO14251 section 3's structured excerpts.

The order's directions about non-agency business and pending grievances, arbitral-award exceptions and unfair-labor-practice proceedings apply to affected employees upon termination of their agreements. caveats: This is the printed substitute amendment, not the parent bill's meaning. It replaces page 1, line 1 through page 60, line 6; adoption at the amendment stage would not itself enact the substitute.

Reports identify amounts, source/country and purpose or intended use. Institutions must retain agreement copies until the latest of four years after agreement, termination, or applicable state retention requirements; produce them for audits or investigations; and translate contracts as applicable. Restricted or conditional gifts also require amounts, dates, conditions, and specified source-country information.

A state or other federal report can replace the disclosure report only if it contains all required information for the same or an equivalent period; state assurances may be required. Institutions must be able to revise past reports to correct errors.

For a knowing or willful disclosure or agreement-copy/translation violation, the Secretary may impose $250 to 50% of the gift or contract amount; three consecutive years permit an additional fine of $100,000 to the gift or contract amount. Knowing or willful foreign-ownership-report violations can incur up to 25% of Higher Education Act funding excluding Title IV student aid, with an additional fine subject to the same 25% cap for three consecutive years of violations. Administrative errors lasting three consecutive years can incur $250 to 50% of the gift or contract amount; two consecutive years without the required gift/contract report can trigger a compliance plan. These are the printed statutory bounds, not a prediction of penalties imposed.

Excluded transactions include student-attendance payments or scholarships from a natural person acting individually, not for another person or entity except the student, without another contract beyond the institution-student attendance agreement; specified intellectual-property licensing or technical assistance not identified as a national-security risk; and funds solely for clinical trials. A U.S.-located institution's purchases of property or services from a foreign source are outside the contract definition. Gifts and contracts through an institution's supporting entities are included. Restricted or conditional gifts/contracts include terms concerning faculty employment, academic or research units/programs, student selection/admission, or aid restricted by the listed country, religion, sex, ethnic-origin or political-opinion categories.

The amendment also incorporates HEA487(e)(2)(B)(ii) gift exceptions: loan/default-prevention/financial-literacy materials and programs; qualifying professional-training food, refreshments and materials; comparable student-employee loan benefits; institution-controlled, non-promotional loan counseling; specified lender/servicer/guarantor philanthropy or contributions without a loan-related advantage; and state-administered education aid. These categories retain the conditions in the incorporated statute, governed here in its 2024 U.S. Code edition.

Institutions must designate a compliance officer, and the Department must maintain an internal, conflict-free contact for compliance assistance and database improvements. Data sharing with outside persons, including political appointees and personnel detailed from other agencies, is limited to expressly authorized or public information. Database user-group composition and meeting mechanics are ancillary to the explanation, not absent from the governed evidence.

Negotiated rules must align with other agencies' reporting under the CHIPS Act, the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, and OSTP guidance including the specified NSPM-33 implementation guidance. Alignment is a rulemaking duty, not an assertion that all reporting regimes become identical. The substitute links Section 117's effective date to the regulations and separately specifies a database deadline relative to the first July 31 after enactment; this candidate does not invent a resolution of that timing interaction.
exact_action_receipts.policy_question: This substitute would require colleges to report foreign gifts and contracts at $100,000 in one year or $250,000 over three years from the same source, while requiring broader disclosures from institutions substantially owned or controlled by foreign sources and for restricted gifts. Reports would become publicly searchable, equivalent state or federal reports could substitute, and specified noncompliance could bring fines or a compliance plan. The proposal includes payment and transaction exclusions and requires negotiated rules to coordinate reporting with other federal research-security requirements before the rewritten disclosure section takes effect.

receipt_projections.question: This substitute would require colleges to report foreign gifts and contracts at $100,000 in one year or $250,000 over three years from the same source, while requiring broader disclosures from institutions substantially owned or controlled by foreign sources and for restricted gifts. Reports would become publicly searchable, equivalent state or federal reports could substitute, and specified noncompliance could bring fines or a compliance plan. The proposal includes payment and transaction exclusions and requires negotiated rules to coordinate reporting with other federal research-security requirements before the rewritten disclosure section takes effect.
receipt_projections.uncertainty_note: This is the printed substitute amendment, not the parent bill's meaning. It replaces page 1, line 1 through page 60, line 6; adoption at the amendment stage would not itself enact the substitute. Reports identify amounts, source/country and purpose or intended use. Institutions must retain agreement copies until the latest of four years after agreement, termination, or applicable state retention requirements; produce them for audits or investigations; and translate contracts as applicable. Restricted or conditional gifts also require amounts, dates, conditions, and specified source-country information. A state or other federal report can replace the disclosure report only if it contains all required information for the same or an equivalent period; state assurances may be required. Institutions must be able to revise past reports to correct errors. For a knowing or willful disclosure or agreement-copy/translation violation, the Secretary may impose $250 to 50% of the gift or contract amount; three consecutive years permit an additional fine of $100,000 to the gift or contract amount. Knowing or willful foreign-ownership-report violations can incur up to 25% of Higher Education Act funding excluding Title IV student aid, with an additional fine subject to the same 25% cap for three consecutive years of violations. Administrative errors lasting three consecutive years can incur $250 to 50% of the gift or contract amount; two consecutive years without the required gift/contract report can trigger a compliance plan. These are the printed statutory bounds, not a prediction of penalties imposed. Excluded transactions include student-attendance payments or scholarships from a natural person acting individually, not for another person or entity except the student, without another contract beyond the institution-student attendance agreement; specified intellectual-property licensing or technical assistance not identified as a national-security risk; and funds solely for clinical trials. A U.S.-located institution's purchases of property or services from a foreign source are outside the contract definition. Gifts and contracts through an institution's supporting entities are included. Restricted or conditional gifts/contracts include terms concerning faculty employment, academic or research units/programs, student selection/admission, or aid restricted by the listed country, religion, sex, ethnic-origin or political-opinion categories. The amendment also incorporates HEA487(e)(2)(B)(ii) gift exceptions: loan/default-prevention/financial-literacy materials and programs; qualifying professional-training food, refreshments and materials; comparable student-employee loan benefits; institution-controlled, non-promotional loan counseling; specified lender/servicer/guarantor philanthropy or contributions without a loan-related advantage; and state-administered education aid. These categories retain the conditions in the incorporated statute, governed here in its 2024 U.S. Code edition. Institutions must designate a compliance officer, and the Department must maintain an internal, conflict-free contact for compliance assistance and database improvements. Data sharing with outside persons, including political appointees and personnel detailed from other agencies, is limited to expressly authorized or public information. Database user-group composition and meeting mechanics are ancillary to the explanation, not absent from the governed evidence. Negotiated rules must align with other agencies' reporting under the CHIPS Act, the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, and OSTP guidance including the specified NSPM-33 implementation guidance. Alignment is a rulemaking duty, not an assertion that all reporting regimes become identical. The substitute links Section 117's effective date to the regulations and separately specifies a database deadline relative to the first July 31 after enactment; this candidate does not invent a resolution of that timing interaction.
